page_hint: Ch 20 §5, Common Mistakes, 'Overlooking data movement cost'
quoted_clause: if every host fetches independently, each query moves its full context bytes, repeated for every query and every host
observed: The sentence implies one query is fetched by every host. In a normal serving fleet a query is routed to one host; independent per-host caches cause repeated fetches across queries and cache misses, not one fetch per host per query.
evidence: The surrounding paragraph is about bytes fetched per query and cross-query overlap. The correct accounting is: one serving host fetches the context for the query it serves; independent caches may duplicate that fetch across queries and hosts when the same context is requested again, but not 'every host' for one query.
root_cause: Conflates per-query fetch with per-host cache replication/miss behavior.
correction: Rewrite to distinguish (a) one fetch by the serving host per query, (b) duplicate fetches across queries when caches are cold or not shared, and (c) replication cost when the same index/context is stored on many hosts. Do not say a single query is fetched by every host.
acceptance_test: The revised paragraph contains no claim that one query is fetched by every host; it separately accounts per-query fetch, cross-query cache reuse, and per-host replication.

page_hint: Ch 22 §8, 'The peak, not the average, sizes the fleet'
quoted_clause: Ch 17's 436 GB of KV per host (640 − 140 − 64) ÷ 24.1 GB/request ≈ 18 in-flight requests per host, and 40 rps × 8.58 s ≈ 343 in flight needs ~19 hosts.
observed: This uses 24.1 GB/request (the 9.2K prompt-only figure) and fractional division to get ~18 slots and ~19 hosts. The canonical whole-slot convention elsewhere uses the 9.5K maximum, 24.9 GB/request, floor(436/24.9)=17 whole slots, and ceil(343/17)=21 hosts. The same inconsistency appears in Ch 24 §3.3, where the 10-rps KV screen is called '~5 hosts' although the canonical 17-slot convention gives ceil(86/17)=6.
evidence: Ch 20 states the canonical KV screen as 21 hosts at 40 rps and ~6 hosts at 10 rps using 17 whole slots. Ch 24 §3.3 check 4 itself uses 24.9 GB and 17 slots to get 21 hosts. Ch 22 §8 and Ch 24 §3.3's average-load discussion use 24.1 GB and fractional slots, producing 18/19 and ~5.
root_cause: Two KV-slot conventions coexist: 9.2K prompt-only fractional GB accounting versus 9.5K-max whole-slot admission. The book has not reconciled them at every anchor.
correction: Use one canonical convention in all fleet-sizing arithmetic: 24.9 GB/request at the 9.5K maximum, floor(436/24.9)=17 whole slots, 10 rps -> 6 hosts, 40 rps -> 21 hosts. If a 9.2K-only no-max variant is intended, label it explicitly as a different scenario and reconcile every dependent host count.
acceptance_test: Recompute every canonical KV host count from the same stated KV-per-request and whole-slot rule. No chapter reports 18/19 hosts for the canonical 40-rps peak or ~5 hosts for the canonical 10-rps average unless it explicitly declares a different scenario.

quoted_clause: decode weight-read per token | ~140 GB | full-weight-read model (70B FP16) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
observed: The 140 GB per token figure is a batch-1 figure. At the canonical host's ~17 concurrent requests, the weight read is amortized across the batch: per-token weight traffic is ~140/17 ≈ 8.2 GB, while the host still reads ~140 GB per decode step. The table labels the batch-1 figure simply 'per token' without the batch-1 qualifier.
evidence: Ch 25 ADR 0017 explicitly distinguishes batch 1 (140 GB weights against ~24.9 GB KV) from C≈17.5 (435.6 GB KV against 140 GB weights). Ch 22's own mental model says 'low-batch decode is bandwidth-bound', but Table 22-1 and the Architecture Consequence drop that qualifier.
root_cause: Batch-1 weight-read traffic is presented as a per-token canonical quantity without carrying its operating-point scope.
correction: Label the 140 GB row as 'batch-1 decode weight-read per token' and add the amortized per-token figure at the canonical concurrency, or replace the row with 'host weight-read per decode step ~140 GB' and state that per-token traffic is 140/C GB. In §6, qualify the 5.6 TB/s rate as the batch-1/host-step rate and note that at C≈17 the per-token weight traffic is ~8.2 GB and arithmetic intensity rises to ~4.3 FLOP/byte.
acceptance_test: Every occurrence of '140 GB per token' or '5.6 TB/s' in Ch 22 states its batch/concurrency scope; no unqualified per-token claim remains.

quoted_clause: a ~21–32-host fleet at the canonical peak (Ch 17/20/24)
observed: The range omits the governing 23-host ρ-derated case-(ii) screen and the 34-host full-policy case-(ii) screen that Ch 20 and Ch 25 report. Ch 24 also summarizes the screens as '21 hosts KV / 19–22 prefill / 32 policy', omitting 23 and 34.
evidence: Ch 20 states: 23 hosts governs before the full policy under case (ii) with ρ=0.95; 34 hosts under 70%×95%+N−1 for case (ii), versus 32 for KV-only. Ch 25 ADR 0015 R1 repeats 21/32 and 22/34.
root_cause: Host-count summaries use different subsets of the screen set without labeling raw versus ρ-derated versus full-policy cases.
correction: Standardize the summary range and label each endpoint: e.g. '21 hosts KV raw; 22 KV with ρ; 23 case-(ii) prefill with ρ; 32 KV full policy; 34 case-(ii) full policy.' Do not use a 21–32 range that excludes 23 and 34.
acceptance_test: All cross-chapter host-count summaries either include 23 and 34 or explicitly state that they are reporting only the raw KV and KV-policy screens.

quoted_clause: leaves Candidate B as a candidate pending measurement — and on check 4 (peak KV residency) neither candidate survives the full screen set at the canonical peak: A fails prefill and KV, B fails peak KV (8 hosts hold 136 — 8 × 17 whole slots — of the 344 in-flight) until sized to ≥21 hosts and re-run.
observed: The paragraph first says Candidate B remains a candidate, then says B as specified (8 hosts) fails peak KV and must be resized to ≥21 hosts. Candidate B at 8 hosts is therefore eliminated, not a surviving candidate.
evidence: The same paragraph says 'neither candidate survives the full screen set at the canonical peak' and 'B fails peak KV ... until sized to ≥21 hosts and re-run.'
root_cause: The outcome conflates 'Candidate B as specified' with 'a resized B configuration'.
correction: State explicitly: Candidate A is eliminated; Candidate B at 8 hosts is also eliminated at the canonical peak; the only surviving object is a resized B (≥21 hosts, plus the prefill screen) that must be benchmarked. Do not call the 8-host B a candidate.
acceptance_test: The outcome paragraph distinguishes B-as-specified from resized-B and does not describe an 8-host B as a surviving candidate.

quoted_clause: 70B dense FP16 deployment (FP16 label; see ADR 0016)
observed: ADR 0016 in the same chapter decides 'Render the serving model in BF16' and says 'this record sets the canonical deployment's precision label to BF16.' The chapter opening still calls the deployment FP16. Many earlier chapters also use '70B dense FP16' as the canonical label.
evidence: ADR 0016 Decision: 'Render the serving model in BF16.' Consequences: 'Accepted, this record sets the canonical deployment's precision label to BF16.' Ch 25 §4 still says '70B FP16 model footprint'.
root_cause: The canonical weight-precision label was not globally reconciled after ADR 0016 introduced BF16.
correction: Choose one canonical label. Either keep the deployment FP16 and make ADR 0016 an illustrative/hypothetical record that does not change the canonical label, or globally update the canonical label to BF16 and explain that all byte-based figures are unchanged because both formats are 2 B/parameter. Update Ch 25 opening and §4 accordingly.
acceptance_test: A global search for '70B dense FP16' and 'BF16' shows one canonical deployment label, with any FP16 references explicitly marked as the alternative or as byte-equivalent.

quoted_clause: its decision body is kept, not rewritten — the status is updated to superseded, with a link to the successor
observed: The record immediately below has Status: HOLD — screened, not committed. The parenthetical says the status is updated to superseded, which contradicts the displayed HOLD status.
evidence: ADR 0015 Status field: 'HOLD — screened, not committed.' The parenthetical describes a supersession event that has not occurred.
root_cause: The prose describes the future supersession rule as if it were the current state.
correction: Change to 'if and when superseded, the status is updated to superseded with a link to the successor' or remove the clause. Keep the displayed status HOLD.
acceptance_test: The prose and the Status field agree: ADR 0015 is HOLD now; supersession is described conditionally.

quoted_clause: the canonical peak already needs 21 hosts on the KV screen (22 under the case (ii) prefill screen; Ch 16/17/20), so 'adding hosts beyond the 21' misunderstands the scale
observed: The same sentence acknowledges that case (ii) needs 22 hosts. If the governing screen is 22 (or 23 with ρ), then adding a host beyond 21 is exactly what the screen requires; it is not a misunderstanding of scale.
evidence: Ch 20 states 22 raw case-(ii) prefill and 23 with ρ; Ch 25 ADR 0015 R1 also carries 22/34. The alternative rejects 'adding capacity' by treating 21 as the scale, while simultaneously naming 22.
root_cause: The alternative uses the KV-only 21-host screen as if it were the governing screen, then mentions the higher prefill screen without reconciling the argument.
correction: Rewrite the alternative to say: adding hosts beyond the governing screen (21 KV raw, 22 case-(ii) raw, 23 with ρ, 32/34 under full policy) is not the first lever for the KV-capacity problem; FP8 KV relaxes the KV ceiling without commissioning new hardware. Do not dismiss the one host needed to meet case (ii) as a misunderstanding.
acceptance_test: The alternative text uses the governing screen consistently and does not call a required case-(ii) host addition a misunderstanding.

quoted_clause: We measure four things continuously: 1. Gate pass rate ... False-promotion rate ... 2. Canary-to-production time and rollback time ... 3. Model freshness / data staleness ... 4. MTTR for a bad release
observed: The list contains at least six distinct metrics: gate pass rate, false-promotion rate, canary-to-production time, rollback time, model freshness/data staleness, and MTTR. Calling them 'four things' is a counting error.
evidence: The enumerated list itself contains two metrics in item 1 and two in item 2, plus items 3 and 4.
root_cause: Grouped metrics are counted as single 'things' without saying so.
correction: Either say 'we measure four groups of things' and keep the grouping, or say 'we measure six metrics' and enumerate them separately.
acceptance_test: The count word matches the number of enumerated metrics or the text explicitly says it is counting groups.
